sources.title: Mobile cinema still has its utility, audience
sources.author: Post News Network
sources.inspection: Fresh direct PDF text retrieval,12pages; targeted text p5 (PDF index4),lines1684–1703; not visual inspection
supported_claims: Retired Dhenkanal district information and public relations employee Lokanath Das recalled putting on village screenings between1978 and1995.
He named Amada Bata and Matira Manisha among films screened.
He recalled travelling by boat to some villages where bridges across Brahmani or Ramial were absent.

The report describes government mobile cinema combining films with information documentaries at the beginning and intervals; public outreach, not an established commercial touring business (lines1660–1683).
limits: Retrospective named employee testimony, not an inspected screening ledger or villagers’ own testimony.
No wage, ticket charge, attendance, film rental/payment or profit evidence. Do not infer paid status from employment title.
Do not generalise newspaper claim of programme ending1995 to all Odisha film outreach.
Do not adopt best-medium rhetoric, causes-of-decline claims, or assume a revived programme exists.

Keep river geography within his recollection of reaching some villages, not a general historical assertion that either river had no bridges. Root independently inspected PDF text; screenshot attempt failed, so no visual verification claimed.

A junior and friends started Film Society of Ravenshaw with his help; report states they screened Spike Lee’s Do the Right Thing on18July2018.

No demonstrated film-career income, fees, attendance or ticket receipts.
Do not repeat dismissive generalisations about young viewers or commercial cinema.
Do not claim planned workshops happened or institutional approaches all succeeded.

recommendation.action: Enhance existing section only, retaining H2 and economics hero; two concrete accounts plus short original economic question. No new article needed.
recommendation.suggested_passage:
In 2020, retired Dhenkanal information and public relations employee Lokanath Das remembered taking films to villages between1978 and1995. He recalled travelling by boat to reach some villages. The government mobile-cinema programme combined films with information documentaries. His remembered programme included Amada Bata and Matira Manisha. Getting those films before viewers required someone to make the journey and put on the show. [audience-mobile-das]

A different kind of organising appears in Abhishek Parija’s2018 account of Film Society Bhubaneswar. He joined its core team after submitting his own film to a festival. He later helped a junior and friends establish a film society at Ravenshaw, where they screened Spike Lee’s Do the Right Thing that July. Watching could lead to discussion—and, for some participants, to helping arrange another screening. [audience-fsb-parija]

These accounts make access tangible without turning it into a box-office claim. They invite a practical economic question: what would let the people who arrange a screening keep doing that work? Transport, a suitable venue, exhibition permission and dependable technical arrangements belong in that conversation alongside ticket sales. The answer will differ between a public outreach programme, a film society and a commercial theatre.
wording_notes: Use existing verified bilingual forms for Amada Bata/Matira Manisha when drafting. Do the Right Thing is English title.
Final paragraph is original proposal/general reasoning, not a claim that either account measured costs or livelihoods.
Avoid an invented boat scene, weather, projector-loading detail or dialogue.
Suggested prose may be expanded through explanation, not extra unverified history.
Link the named adaptations to existing Kalindi and Basanta profiles if useful; no need another adaptation synopsis.
